extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of Indian literature; writers studying Premchand and Hindi–Urdu social fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative features relevant to producing fiction in the manner of Munshi Premchand — i.e., Hindi/Urdu social realism focused on village/urban poor, caste, women's plight and political themes. Useful for writers aiming to emulate Premchand or critics assessing works against his standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Premchand is considered the first Hindi author whose writings prominently featured realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize realistic depiction of life rather than romantic or fantastical elements; ground scenes, characters and social relations in observable social conditions. Examples: his novels describe the problems of the poor and the urban middle-class; social realism was his preferred aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social themes / arousing public awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: He used literature for the purpose of arousing public awareness about national and social issues and often wrote about topics related to corruption, child widowhood, prostitution, feudal system, poverty, colonialism and on the Indian independence movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center narratives on social problems and reformist concerns; choose topics such as corruption, dowry, widowhood, child exploitation, poverty and colonial oppression. Stories and novels should make readers conscious of these issues (e.g., Premashram, Nirmala, Karmabhoomi, Godaan, Kafan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on peasants, labourers, women and caste hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: He was one of the first authors to write about caste hierarchies and the plight of women and labourers of the late 1880s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the lived experience, aspirations and constraints of peasants, workers and marginalized castes and genders. Use concrete domestic and rural/urban details (e.g., Godaan's Hori longing for a cow, Idgah, Kafan) to illuminate social injustice and human dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalistic outlook and critique of religious hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: His works depict a rationalistic outlook, which views religious values as something that allows the powerful hypocrites to exploit the weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a critical stance toward institutions and beliefs when they function to oppress; expose hypocrisy rather than celebrating piety uncritically. Use characters and incidents to show how religious pretence can mask exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement and patriotic overtones
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Premchand's early short stories had patriotic overtones, influenced by the Indian independence movement; he supported greater political freedom and engaged with political thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate political concerns (nationalism, reform, critique of colonial rule) into plots and character motivations. Political messages can be explicit but may also be woven into social narratives; examples include early patriotic stories and the banned Soz-e-Watan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, allegory or disguised settings to evade censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: He satirised the Indians who cooperated with the British Government. He did not specifically mention the British in some of his stories because of strong government censorship but disguised his opposition in settings from the medieval era and foreign history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct critique is risky, use historical, medieval or foreign settings, allegory or satire to convey dissent. Satire may target collaborators, complacency or social elites while avoiding direct naming when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Village life as stage for complex drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In his last days, he focused on village life as a stage for complex drama, as seen in the novel Godaan and the short-story collection Kafan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the village as a microcosm where economic, social and moral conflicts intersect; show how local institutions, customs and interpersonal ties create dramatic tension and ethical dilemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of economic conditions and critique of industrialisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Premchand was focused on the economic liberalisation of the peasantry and the working class and opposed rapid industrialisation, which he felt would hurt the interests of the peasants and lead to the oppression of the workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore economic structures (zamindari, land tenure, labor exploitation, effects of mills/factories) and their human consequences. Position characters within these economic pressures rather than treating economics as mere background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotyped characters; aim for balanced, well-structured narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics noted early works 'lack a good plot and feature stereotyped characters' and later works (e.g., Godaan) are praised as 'well-structured and well-balanced' though some earlier novels had 'structural flaws' and 'too many authorial explanations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters with complexity and avoid flat stereotypes; structure the narrative for balance and clarity; resist over-explaining or authorial intrusions—let actions and situations reveal social truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and adaptation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Premchand translated several non-Hindi works into Hindi (Dickens, Wilde, Galsworthy, Tolstoy, Guy de Maupassant, etc.) and adapted foreign literature for Indian readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or adapting, localize themes and particulars to make foreign works resonate with local social realities; translations and adaptations are part of literary practice and influence voice and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrative to combine social chronicling with literary craft
rubrics_metrics.description: He comes across as a 'superb social chronicler' who lifted fiction in Hindi and Urdu to a high level of realistic narrative comparable to European fiction of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance documentary social observation with literary elements (character development, plot control, thematic coherence). Aim for writing that functions both as social record and artful storytelling.
